title: Where is the universe's missing matter? Scientists have found a way to track it down
summary: Researchers combined 2,870 fast radio bursts observed by CHIME with positions of over 6 million galaxies from DESI to map diffuse halos of ordinary matter stretching millions of light years from galaxies. The study shows energetic processes such as black hole jets and stellar explosions can expel baryons far into intergalactic space, offering a new way to locate the universe's missing ordinary matter.
content:
Missing matter doesn’t always mean invisible dark matter. It could be the same stuff that makes up stars and planets, yet a large portion of such matter remains undetected. Now, researchers from the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME)/Fast Radio Bursts Collaboration, including McGill University and MIT, have developed a new method to hunt down the universe's long-missing ordinary matter by combining galaxy locations with ultrabright flashes of radio waves known as fast radio bursts (FRBs). The researchers have reported their findings in a paper published in the Physical Review Letters.

First discovered in 2007, FRBs are incredibly bright flashes of radio waves that last only a few thousandths of a second before disappearing. These signals travel across vast stretches of space and pass through clouds of gas and scattered particles before reaching Earth. This interaction causes the radio waves to spread out slightly, an effect astronomers call smearing. The more matter an FRB encounters, the greater the smearing becomes.

The team realized that these bursts could serve as natural probes of the invisible material filling the universe. The researchers studied 2,870 fast radio bursts detected by the CHIME/FRB collaboration. The results portrayed a stunning picture of missing matter that forms diffuse halos, extending far beyond galaxies and galaxy groups. "We find that, overall, where there are more galaxies, there tends to be more missing matter around them," says Haochen Wang, a graduate student in MIT’s Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, in a statement.

The team found that higher-energy (blue) components of FRBs are less affected by the missing matter and arrive sooner at detectors than the more smeared lower-energy (red) components. By measuring each FRB’s wavelength-dependent delay, the scientists were able to estimate how much matter the radio waves traversed before reaching CHIME. The researchers then linked these dispersion measurements with the locations of over 6 million galaxies cataloged by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) in Tucson.

Comparing FRB dispersion with galaxy positions revealed a clear association: missing ordinary matter is not confined to galactic disks but is scattered into diffuse puffs and halos that stretch roughly four million light years from galaxies. The pattern implies that energetic processes inside galaxies—including jets from accreting black holes and powerful stellar explosions—are more efficient at expelling gas into intergalactic space than previously appreciated. "We are finding that the activity in galaxies is messier than we thought," Wang adds. "They’re more like fountains, and really push out gas to very large distances."

Beyond locating the missing baryons, the study serves as proof that fast radio bursts can be used as cosmic probes of otherwise invisible matter, opening a new observational window on the distribution and movement of ordinary matter across large scales of the universe.
